blocks.content: The previous topics covered primary keys, foreign keys, and candidate and composite keys, the actual mechanisms a relational database uses, this topic steps back to name the three shapes of relationship those mechanisms are built to represent, one to one, one to many, and many to many.

This topic covers each relationship type with a concrete example, how the choice of relationship shape directly determines your table design, and why getting this choice wrong early tends to cause real problems later.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438608352-45633234.png
1. One to One Relationships
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438608355-812851917.png

A one to one relationship means exactly one row in one table corresponds to exactly one row in another table, a users table and a user_profiles table split this way, one profile row per user, is a common example, often used to separate frequently accessed data from rarely accessed data.
2. One to Many Relationships
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438608355-984576840.png

A one to many relationship means one row in one table can correspond to many rows in another table, one customer places many orders, one blog post has many comments, this is the most common relationship shape in a typical schema, and it is exactly what a plain foreign key column represents directly.
{"headers":["Relationship Type","Example"],"rows":[["One to one","A user and their single profile row"],["One to many","A customer and their many orders"]]}
3. Many to Many Relationships
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438608355-957644325.png

A many to many relationship means many rows in one table can correspond to many rows in another table, one student enrolls in many courses, and one course has many students, this is exactly the enrollments example covered in the previous Candidate and Composite Keys topic.
4. One to One vs One to Many
blocks.text: 4. One to One vs One to Many

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438608356-275105156.png
blocks.alt: One to One vs One to Many

blocks.content: One to one relationships are genuinely less common than one to many, most real relationships involve one side having many of the other, a one to one split is usually a deliberate design choice, separating optional or sensitive columns into their own table, rather than the natural shape data falls into.

{"headers":["Relationship Type","How It Is Implemented"],"rows":[["One to one","A foreign key column that is also declared UNIQUE"],["Many to many","A junction table holding a foreign key to each side"]]}
5. How Many to Many Actually Gets Implemented
blocks.text: 5. How Many to Many Actually Gets Implemented

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438608356-695724011.png
blocks.alt: How Many to Many Actually Gets Implemented

blocks.content: A relational database has no direct way to store a many to many relationship on its own, it is always implemented as a junction table, exactly the enrollments table from the previous topic, sitting between the two tables and holding a foreign key to each, which turns one many to many relationship into two separate one to many relationships.
The junction table pattern
6. Implementing a One to One Relationship
blocks.text: 6. Implementing a One to One Relationship

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438608356-940592410.png
blocks.alt: Implementing a One to One Relationship

blocks.content: A one to one relationship is implemented as a foreign key column that is also declared UNIQUE, a plain foreign key alone only enforces one to many, adding the UNIQUE constraint on top is what actually restricts each referenced row to at most one referencing row.

blocks.title: The UNIQUE constraint is the entire difference here
blocks.content: A user_profiles table with a plain, non unique user_id foreign key column technically allows one to many, adding UNIQUE on that same column is the single change that correctly enforces one to one.
7. Choosing the Right Relationship Early
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438608356-733723995.png

Choosing the wrong relationship shape early, treating something that is genuinely many to many as one to many for instance, tends to force awkward workarounds later, once real data and real application code already depend on the incorrect structure, working through the actual relationship shape carefully before creating tables saves significant rework.

blocks.title: Ask how many rows on each side, concretely
blocks.content: A reliable way to determine relationship shape is asking directly, can one row on side A relate to more than one row on side B, and can one row on side B relate to more than one row on side A, the answer to those two questions determines the shape precisely.
8. Common Mistakes

["Modeling a many to many relationship as a plain one to many foreign key, then hitting data integrity problems","Forgetting the UNIQUE constraint needed to properly enforce a one to one relationship","Splitting a table into a one to one relationship without a genuine reason, adding unnecessary joins for no real benefit","Not identifying the relationship shape before designing the tables, then restructuring later under pressure"]
items: Modeling a many to many relationship as a plain one to many foreign key, then hitting data integrity problems
Forgetting the UNIQUE constraint needed to properly enforce a one to one relationship
Splitting a table into a one to one relationship without a genuine reason, adding unnecessary joins for no real benefit
Not identifying the relationship shape before designing the tables, then restructuring later under pressure

blocks.content: 9. Key Takeaways

["One to one, one to many, and many to many are the three fundamental relationship shapes in relational design","A plain foreign key column naturally represents one to many, adding UNIQUE turns that same structure into one to one","A many to many relationship always requires a junction table, turning it into two separate one to many relationships","The next topic, ER Diagrams, covers how to visually map out these relationships before writing a single CREATE TABLE statement"]
items: One to one, one to many, and many to many are the three fundamental relationship shapes in relational design
A plain foreign key column naturally represents one to many, adding UNIQUE turns that same structure into one to one
A many to many relationship always requires a junction table, turning it into two separate one to many relationships
